p_question-5864.ja:
以下は、新聞のコラムである。


　毎日の生活の中で、天気予報は欠かせない情報の一つだ。着る服装を選ぶときも、休日の予定を立てる時も、天気は[48]。毎朝天気予報をチェックしている人も多いだろう。

　そんな天気予報を活用した新たな取り組みが始まっている。気象情報から食品の高度な需要予測を行い、「食品ロス」、つまり、まだ食べられるのに捨てられてしまう食品を減らすというものだ。

　食品の中には、天候や気温に需要が大きく左右されるものも多い。需要予測を誤り、過剰に生産してしまうと、それだけ多くの食品ロスが生じてしまう。

　[49]政府は、気象データとPOSデータ（何が、いつ、いくつ、いくらで売れたのかを示す販売情報）から高度な需要予測を行い、製造や販売の各社に提供する取り込みを始めた。その結果は、食品ロスを減らせるばかりではない。食品が無駄に捨てられることが少なくなるため、その処理の過程で発生する二酸化炭素を減らすこともできる。

　[50]、まず、長期保存が出来ず気象状況が売り上げに大きく影響する「豆腐」と、特定の季節に需要が集中する「麺つゆ」に絞って実験が行われた。その結果、食品ロスを20〜30%減らせることがわかった。現在は、対象商品を拡大しながら、人工知能も取り入れ、さらに高度な需要予測が可能になってきているという。このように、私たちの生活に欠かせない気象情報は、食品ロス問題の解決にも役立っているのである。

　今後、より大きな成果が[51]。

p_question-5868.ja:
(1)　以下は、保護者に向けて書かれた文書である。

　最初に知っておきたいのは、保護者が嫌いなものは、子供も好きになれないということである。普段から「まずい、嫌い」と聞かされているものを美味しいと思えないのは当然です。また嫌がるものを無理に食べさせても、嫌な思い出が残るばかりで、良い結果は出ません。

　それに対して、最初は苦手だった食べ物でも、周囲の大人たちが「美味しいね」と笑顔で食べている姿を見て興味が湧き、食べられるようになることがあります。つまり、偏食をなくすには、「親子で一緒に楽しみながら」がコツなのだ。

(1)　The following document is addressed to parents and guardians.

　The first thing to understand is that if a parent dislikes something, a child will not easily come to like it either. It’s only natural that a child cannot find tasty what they constantly hear called “yucky” or “I hate it.” Forcing a child to eat what they dislike only leaves unpleasant memories and produces no good results.

　Conversely, even foods a child initially struggles with can become acceptable when they see the adults around them eating with smiles and saying, “This is delicious,” which sparks their curiosity. In short, to reduce picky eating, the key is for parent and child to enjoy eating together.

p_question-5869.ja:

p_question-5870.ja:
(3)

　私は毎日、自宅の周りを散歩する。運動、気分転換など色々な理由はあるが、コンビニに立ち寄ることも目的の一つだ。

　そこでいろいろな売り物を見て、雑誌を眺めて、飲み物を買う。この飲み物一つとっても、世の中の様々な流れが凝縮されている（注1）。

　例えば、大きさ。ペットボトルと言えば500ccと思い込んでいるかもしれないが、昨年辺りから変化がある。400cc前後に減量しているものがあるのだ。でも、値段は同じ。

　割高（注2）なようだが、結構人気がある。理由は簡単。女性がバッグに入れやすいのだ。

（注1）凝縮されている：たくさんのものが一つのところにぎゅっと詰まっている。（注2）割高：分量に対して値段が高いこと。

(3)

　I take a walk around my neighborhood every day. I have various reasons—exercise, a change of pace—but stopping by the convenience store is one of my aims as well.

　There I look over the various goods, browse magazines, and buy a drink. Even a single beverage reflects (Note 1) many of the currents in society in condensed form.

　For example, size. You may assume a PET bottle means 500 cc, but there’s been a change since about last year: some have been reduced to around 400 cc—yet the price is the same.

　It may seem pricier for the amount (Note 2), but it’s quite popular. The reason is simple: it fits easily into women’s handbags.

(Note 1) condensed: many things tightly packed into one.(Note 2) pricier: the price is high relative to the quantity.

p_question-5872.ja:
(5)　以下の文章は、就職に対する学生の意識調査の結果について書かれたものである。

　今回の調査では、入社する企業を決めるうえで重視する点を最大三つ挙げてもらった。企業の規模や将来性、希望職種に就ける可能性などを抑えてトップになったのは「社員の魅力や社内の雰囲気」（54.3%）。「勤務地や転勤の有無」も22.1%あった。良好な人間関係や居心地の良さを求める学生が増えているようだ。

(5)　The following passage reports results from a survey of students’ attitudes toward employment.

　In this survey, respondents listed up to three points they prioritize when choosing a company to join. Surpassing factors such as company size, future prospects, and the chance of being assigned to a desired job type, the top response was “the appeal of employees and the in-house atmosphere” (54.3%). “Work location and whether transfers are required” also garnered 22.1%. It appears more students are seeking good human relationships and a comfortable workplace environment.

p_question-5873.ja:
（１）

　書くという行為は、最終的には、不特定多数の読者に向けられている。しかし、そのプロセスにおいては、実は、かなり具体的な相手に向かって書いているところがあるのだ。　実際に書き進める際には、私の場合、その原稿を読む最初の読者、すなわち担当編集者を念頭（注１）に置きながら書いている。ある意味で、その人に向けて書いている部分もかなりあるのだ。編集者がつまらない反応をしそうだと、こちらのやる気も落ちてくるというようなことが実際にはある。逆に言うと、編集者とはそれくらい重要な仕事だと私は思う。

（中略）

　大学で教えていたときにこんなことがあった。よく質問してくる学生がいて、それがいつもたいへんおもしろい質問なのだ。だんだん「この学生はなかなか可能性がある」と思うようになって、その学生が期末にどんなレポートを書いてくるか楽しみにしていたら、レポートがすごくつまらなかったのである。なぜか、おそらくはこうだ。その学生は、質問している時には具体的な他者、すなわち私に向かってしゃべっている。そのときの方が思考が刺激されておもしろい論点に自分で気がつくのだが、いざ（注２）レポートを書く際には一般論みたいに書かなければいけないという構え（注３）になり、そうなったとたんに、急に頭が固くなってしまったのだろう。

　本や論文は、最終的には誰に向かって語っているかわからないようなスタイルで書かれることが普通だけれども、そこには対話がないといけない。要するに、人に話したくなるようなことじゃないと書いても意味がないと思うのだ。

（注１）念頭に置く：ここでは、意識する（注２）いざ：ここでは、実際に（注３）構え：ここでは、気持ち

(1)

　Writing, in the end, is directed at an unspecified number of readers. Yet in the process, one is in fact often writing to a fairly specific person.　When I actually proceed with a piece, in my case I write with the first reader of the manuscript—namely, the commissioning editor—in mind (Note 1). In a sense, a substantial portion is addressed to that person. In reality, if I anticipate a dull reaction from the editor, my motivation drops. Conversely, that is how important the editor’s role is, in my view.

(Omitted)

　When I was teaching at a university, this happened: there was a student who asked questions frequently, and they were always very interesting. I gradually came to think, “This student has real potential,” and looked forward to the student’s term-end report—only for the report to be extremely boring. Why? Probably this: when the student was asking questions, they were speaking to a concrete other—that is, to me. In those moments their thinking was stimulated, and they themselves noticed interesting points. But when it came (Note 2) time to write the report, they adopted the stance (Note 3) that it had to be written like a general discussion; at that point their mind must have suddenly stiffened.

　Books and papers are usually written in a style that doesn’t make clear whom they are addressing, but even so, there must be a sense of dialogue. In short, if it isn’t something you feel like telling someone, there’s no point in writing it.

(Note 1) keep in mind: here, to be conscious of(Note 2) when it comes to: here, actually(Note 3) stance: here, frame of mind

p_question-5876.ja:
（２）

　個性の重視ということが注目されるようになって以来、「子供の興味を尊重し、一人一人の子供が興味を持つこと、「やってみたい」ということを好きにやらせることが、個性の重視である。」という解釈が広がりました。しかしその結果、社会生活上のしきたり（注１）や習慣を教える機会を失ったと悩む教師と、好きなことしかやりたがらない子供をつくってしまったということはないでしょうか。個性の重視とは、「二人と同じ人間はいない、つまり一人一人異なる存在である。だから、一人一人が異なった興味や価値観を持つのは当然である。」という考え方を肯定する人間観を意味しているのです。

（中略）

　子供の興味や関心は日々変化する可能性があります。しかし、何らか（注２）の形でその対象を知る機会がなかったなら、興味を持つこともないのです。小学生はまだまだ経験の幅が狭いものです。ですから、おのずと（注３）興味や関心を持つ対象も、非常に限られた範囲のものになります。さまざまなものに興味を持つのを持つばかりでなく、興味が持てるように、さまざまな体験ができるようにすることが大切です。

（注１）しきたり：昔からの決まり（注２）何らかの：何かの（注３）おのずと：自然と

(2)

　Since attention began to focus on “respecting individuality,” an interpretation has spread that says: “Respect a child’s interests and let each child freely do what they are interested in and ‘want to try’; that is what it means to value individuality.” But has this not resulted in teachers lamenting that they have lost opportunities to teach social conventions (Note 1) and customs, and in producing children who only want to do what they like? To value individuality means a view of human beings that affirms the idea that no two people are the same—that each person is different—and therefore it is natural that each person has different interests and values.

(Omitted)

　Children’s interests can change from day to day. However, if they have no opportunity in some form (Note 2) to become acquainted with a given object or activity, they will not develop an interest in it. Elementary school children still have a narrow range of experience. Consequently, the objects of their interests naturally (Note 3) fall within a very limited scope. It is important not only to encourage interest in many things, but also to provide varied experiences so they can come to take an interest in them.

(Note 1) conventions: long-standing rules(Note 2) in some form: in some way(Note 3) naturally: of its own accord

p_question-5879.ja:
（３）

　イヌの散歩をしていると、最近ではイヌも挨拶の仕方を忘れてしまったのではないかと思ってしまいます。集団行動を経験したことがあるイヌ、もしくは（注１）、飼い主からイヌらしい教育を受けて順位制（注２）を感じることができるようになったイヌは、道でほかのイヌにすれ違い近づいたときには挨拶らしいことをします。ところが、集団行動の経験もなく、家でも甘やかされて育ったイヌは、現代のヒト社会のように挨拶をしないように見えます。挨拶をするイヌが、ほかの挨拶なしのイヌに対して威嚇する（注３）ことが観察されます。ところが、この挨拶犬が子イヌと遭遇したときには、子イヌが挨拶をできなくても威嚇をしないことが多いのです。挨拶犬にとって子イヌであるというシグナルがなんなのかわかりませんが、とにかく子イヌと成犬とを区別したうえで挨拶のあるなしを判断しているようです。

　イヌの挨拶行動は、生得的（注４）あるいは習得的（学習的）のどちらでしょうか？順位制にしたがった行動ができるようになったイヌでは、イヌ社会での経験がなくてもある程度の挨拶行動ができることから、生得的であるといえます。また、より儀式的な挨拶行動が円滑に（注５）実行されるためには、ほかのイヌとの集団生活があったほうがよいことから、習得的な部分もあるといえるでしょう。

（注１）もしくは：または（注２）順位制：上下関係にもとづいてできた順序の決まり（注３）威嚇する：ここでは、ほえて相手を怖がらせる（注４）生得的：生まれたときから持っている（注５）円滑に：スムーズに、滑らかに

(3)

　When I walk my dog these days, I sometimes think dogs have forgotten how to greet one another. Dogs that have experienced group living—or (Note 1) that have received dog-appropriate training from their owners and learned to perceive hierarchy (Note 2)—perform something like a greeting when they pass and approach other dogs on the street. By contrast, dogs with no experience of group life and raised indulgently at home seem not to greet, much like people in modern human society. It has been observed that greeting dogs will threaten (Note 3) other dogs that fail to greet. However, when such a greeting dog encounters a puppy, it often does not threaten even if the puppy fails to greet. We don’t know what signals a “puppy” to the greeting dog, but in any case it seems to distinguish between puppies and adult dogs and then decide whether a greeting is present.

　Are dogs’ greeting behaviors innate (Note 4) or acquired (learned)? In dogs that can act according to a rank order, some greeting behavior appears even without experience in dog society, suggesting it is innate. At the same time, because more ritualized greeting behaviors are executed more smoothly (Note 5) when there has been group living with other dogs, there are clearly acquired elements as well.

(Note 1) or: alternatively(Note 2) rank order: rules based on hierarchical relationships(Note 3) threaten: here, bark to intimidate the other(Note 4) innate: present from birth(Note 5) smoothly: in a fluid manner

p_question-5882.ja:
A


　子供に特定のスポーツを習わせる家庭が多い。早くから一つのスポーツを集中的に練習させることで、子供の才能を伸ばしたいという親の気持ちは理解できるが、子供の体への負担が大きいことが心配だ。同じ動きを繰り返し練習することになり、けがをしやすくなるからだ。まだ成長の途中の子どもにとってまず必要なのは、さまざまなスポーツを通して、多様な動きを身につけることではないだろうか。得意な動きも苦手な動きも行うことによって、全身の運動能力をバランスよく向上させられる。専門的な技術の習得は、その後でも遅くはないのだ。

A


　Many families have their children learn a particular sport. While I understand parents’ desire to develop their children’s talents by having them intensely practice a single sport from an early age, I worry about the heavy burden on their bodies. Repeating the same motions leads to a higher risk of injury. For children who are still growing, what they need first is to acquire a variety of movements through various sports. By performing both movements they are good at and those they are not, they can improve overall physical abilities in a well-balanced way. Learning specialized techniques can come later without being too late.

p_question-5886.ja:
かつては学校を卒業したら、それから30年か40年の人生を考えればよかったのです。 今は学校を出ても、これから後80年近い人生を考えなければいけないかもしれません。私 達を待ち伏せ（注1）している人生の時間が、とんでもなく長くなっています。うかつに（注2）、 歳もとれなくなっているのです。

　100年前、人生50年と言われた時代には、どんなことをするのにもとんでもない時間が もったいないぐらいかかってしまいました。自動車がなかった。飛行機がなかった。どこへ ゆくのにも、今から考えればとんでもない時間がかかっています。それがあっという間にど んどん遠くなった。新幹線ができた。かつては動くことだけではなくて、何をするのにも、 どこへ行くのにも時間を考えなければならなかったのです。いろいろなことをするというの は、時間のかかることをあえてすることでした。漬物には季節が一つ必要でした。人生は短 かった時に、何かするのに、それだけ長い時間が必要でした。ですから、①退屈する前に、 時間は過ぎたのです。

　昔から一泊か二泊を要したところへ、今は日帰りで行って帰ってくるということをしてい る。そんなに時間を惜しんで、物事を急いでして、しかも昔の人の生きたのよりもその二倍 に近いような、長い長い人生を送らなければいけないとしたら、②時間がむしろ負担になっ てくるかもしれません。便利になって時間がどんどん節約されてきた。ところが、一生の時 間の方はどんどん長くなった。そうすると、どういうことになるでしょうか。使わない時 間、もてあます時間、何もしない時間、極端に言うと、何をしていいのかわからない時間が どんどん増えてくる、ということです。

　私たちの人生は、先に途方もない時間が待っている人生です。そうしたことを考えるとき に、ますます重要になってくるのが、私の考えでは読書です。私たちの人生に否応なく割り 込んできてしまう、この途方もない長さの時間に、じゅうぶんに耐えられるだけのソフトウ ェア（注3）を持っている、それどころかどんなに一生ぜんぶを使っても絶対に使い切れな いほどソフトウェアを持っているのは本しかないからです。何にせよ本というソフトウェアは 10年や30年の産物ではないのです。すくなく見積もっても、3000年かけて作られつ づけているのです。

（注1）待ち伏せする：かくれて待つ
（注2）うかつに：うっかり
（注3）ソフトウェア：ここでは知識などの内容を指す

In the past, after graduating from school you only had to think about the next 30 or 40 years of life. Now, even after finishing school, you may have to plan for nearly 80 years ahead. The span of life time lying in wait for us (Note 1) has become extraordinarily long. We can no longer, carelessly (Note 2), even grow old the way we used to.

　A hundred years ago, in an era when people spoke of “fifty years of life,” everything took an astonishingly long time—so long it felt wasteful. There were no cars. There were no airplanes. Going anywhere took, from today’s perspective, an incredible amount of time. Then, before we knew it, those distances shrank. The bullet train appeared. In the past, not only moving from place to place but doing anything at all required careful thought about time. Doing various things meant deliberately taking on time-consuming tasks. Making pickles required an entire season. When life was short, doing anything required that much more time. Therefore, ① time passed before we had a chance to get bored.

　Places that once required an overnight or two can now be visited and returned from in a day. If we are to save time so fiercely, rush everything, and on top of that live a life nearly twice as long as people did in the past, ② time itself may become a burden. Life has grown convenient and time is increasingly saved; yet the time of a lifetime has grown longer and longer. What follows? Unused time, time to kill, time doing nothing—in the extreme, more and more time when we don’t even know what to do.

　Ours is a life with a vast stretch of time ahead. In thinking about that, what becomes ever more important, in my view, is reading. Only books possess the “software” (Note 3)—the content—to withstand this tremendous length of time that wedges itself into our lives whether we like it or not; indeed, only books have such an abundance of software that no matter how much of one’s life you spend, you will never exhaust it. In any case, the software we call books is not the product of ten or thirty years. Even at the most modest estimate, it has been in continual creation for three thousand years.

(Note 1) lie in wait: to wait in hiding
(Note 2) carelessly: thoughtlessly, inadvertently
(Note 3) software: here, the content of knowledge, etc.

In the context of the sentence, "ちょうどいい（　　　）で警官が通りかかったので、助かった。" the speaker expresses relief due to a policeman coincidentally passing by at an opportune moment. The word "タイミング" (timing) appropriately describes a specific moment or point in time when something happens. This aligns perfectly with the idea of "just the right timing" which brings about the beneficial outcome of encountering help.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: タイマー (タイマー) means "timer." A timer refers to a device or tool that measures time, which doesn't conceptually fit with the idea of encountering a policeman at an opportune moment.
- Answer 2: アクシデント (アクシデント) means "accident." An accident describes an unforeseen and often unfortunate event, which doesn't match the context of finding help at the right moment.
- Answer 4: アクション (アクション) means "action." While this refers to the act of doing something, it doesn't convey the sense of timing or coincidental perfectness needed in this context.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The word タイミング is often used in Japanese to discuss the appropriateness or advantage of when an event occurs. Recognizing loanwords like these, derived from English, can help in quickly identifying the right context during comprehension tests.

Answer 1: がっかりした is correct. It means "felt disappointed," which is a direct paraphrase of 失望した (shitsubou shita) meaning "was disappointed."

**Question Translation**  
"I was disappointed by that person's cold attitude."

**Explanation**  
The phrase 失望した (shitsubou shita) directly translates to "was disappointed." The word がっかりした (gakkari shita) also means "felt disappointed" or "was let down," which makes it a perfect paraphrase given the context of disappointment expressed due to the cold attitude.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: びっくりした (bikkuri shita) means "was surprised" or "was shocked." This does not align with the feeling of disappointment expressed by 失望した.
- Answer 3: かっとした (katto shita) suggests "flared up" or "got angry," which indicates a sudden, intense reaction, not the sense of disappointment that 失望した conveys.
- Answer 4: ぞっとした (zotto shita) implies "felt a chill" or "was frightened." It usually conveys an element of fear or dread, which is not relevant to disappointment.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
失望 (shitsubou) and がっかり both convey the idea of unmet expectations leading to disappointment. The use of different verbs (した) maintains the same tense and emotional tone, making these words suitable paraphrases for each other.

questions.stem: 引用
opts: プレゼンが上手い先輩のやり方を引用
大きな川から水を引用
レポートで、新聞記事を引用
ほかの人のお金を引用
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
引用（いんよう） — to quote, to cite

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
In the report, I quote a newspaper article.

**Explanation**  
The word **引用** is used to express the act of quoting or citing something, typically in a written or verbal context. "新聞記事を引用する" (to quote a newspaper article) is a common and appropriate usage of 引用, as it involves taking text or statements from a source.

**Other Options**

① プレゼンが上手い先輩のやり方を引用する。  
→ I quote the methods of a senior who is good at presentations.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
"引用する" is not typically used to describe methods or ways of doing something. A more suitable verb would be "参考にする" (to refer) or "取り入れる" (to adopt).

② 大きな川から水を引用する。  
→ I quote water from a big river.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"引用" is not applicable to physical objects like water. The correct term would be "取水する" (to draw water) or simply "川から水を引く" for water collection or usage.

④ ほかの人のお金を引用してはいけない。  
→ You should not quote other people's money.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"引用" cannot be used with money. A phrase like "使ってはいけない" (should not use) or "借りる" (to borrow) would make sense instead.

**Usage Note**  
"引用" is almost exclusively employed in contexts involving text, speech, or any situation where a statement or idea is taken from another source and used for presentation or argumentation. It's unsuitable for physical items, actions, or money.

오답: 1 「やり方を引用」(방식을 인용)은 어색, 보통 「参考にする」. 2 川에서 물 끌어오기는 「引(ひ)く」. 4 돈을 끌어오는 것에는 「引用」 안 씀.

なくしたと思った大事な本が見つかって、ほっと
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
ほっと — a feeling of relief

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
When I found the important book I thought I had lost, I felt relieved.

**Explanation**  
The word **ほっと** accurately describes a feeling of relief or a sense of release from tension. It is often used in situations where something worrying or concerning gets resolved, such as finding a lost item or receiving good news.

**Other Options**

① ほっと気づいたら、ポケットの中のかぎがなかった。  
→ Suddenly, I realized there was no key in my pocket.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
"ほっと" is incorrectly used here as it implies relief, but realizing you've misplaced something typically doesn’t bring relief. A better choice would be "ふと" (suddenly) or "気づいたら" (when I realized).

② 会議中にほっとしていたら、上司に注意された。  
→ I felt relieved during the meeting, and the boss warned me.  
🔶 Awkward Usage    
Using "ほっとしていた" suggests relief, but being relaxed during a meeting in a way that attracts a boss's warning does not logically connect to relief. "ぼんやりしていた" (daydreaming) fits better in this context.

③ 好きな人に話しかけられて、ほっと顔が赤くなった。  
→ When the person I like spoke to me, I felt relieved and blushed.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"ほっと" is not appropriate for describing an emotional reaction involving attraction or embarrassment. "どきっと" (startled or surprised) would better convey the sudden emotional effect of being spoken to by someone you like.

**Usage Note**  
"ほっと" is most effective in contexts where an issue is resolved or a worry is alleviated. It is not suitable for sudden surprise, realization, embarrassment, or unrelated casual observations.

questions.stem: 展開
opts: 高橋教授は、この島で生物の展開
この漫画は、ストーリーの展開
好きなことをしている時は、時間の展開
池田選手はとても強くて、５年連続で決勝戦への展開
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
展開（てんかい） — development, unfolding, progression

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
This manga's story development is interesting.

**Explanation**  
The word **展開** refers to the process of something evolving or progressing, often used in contexts like stories, events, or situations. "ストーリーの展開" (story development) is a common and natural expression in Japanese, as it describes how a narrative unfolds or progresses over time.

**Other Options**

① 高橋教授は、この島で生物の__展開__の歴史を調べている。  
→ Professor Takahashi is studying the history of the development of organisms on this island.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
While "展開" can relate to development, "生物の展開" is not the typical expression. A more natural word would be "進化" (evolution) or "発展" (development).

③ 好きなことをしている時は、時間の__展開__が早い。  
→ When doing things you like, time's development is fast.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"展開" is not used for time. "時間が経つのが早い" (time passes quickly) captures the intended meaning.

④ 池田選手はとても強くて、５年連続で決勝戦への__展開__を決めている。  
→ Ikeda is very strong and has secured progression to the finals for five consecutive years.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"展開" is not appropriate for describing competition progressions. "進出" (advancement) or "到達" (reaching) would be a better fit for this context.

**Usage Note**  
"展開" typically aligns with situations where development or progression of a sequence of events occurs, such as narratives or plots in stories. It does not apply to abstract concepts like time or competition phases.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 — 「만화는 스토리의 展開(전개)가 재미있다」. 「展開(てんかい)」=전개, 진전.
오답: 1 教授가 생물의 '전개'는 의미 불명. 3 시간의 '전개'는 「経過」. 4 결승전으로의 '전개'는 「進出」이 자연.
포인트: 「展開」는 이야기·상황·논의가 펼쳐지는 변화. 「ストーリー·議論·事態の展開」.

questions.stem: 妥当
opts: 品質に比べて値段が高いと言う人もいるが、私は妥当
風邪気味だったので、今日の会議が中止になったのは、私には妥当
旅行の日は雨の予報だったが、きれいに晴れて、妥当
この曲は、歌詞が今の私の気持ちに妥当
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
妥当（だとう） — reasonable, appropriate, fair

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
Some people say the price is high for the quality, but I think it's a reasonable amount.

**Explanation**  
The word **妥当** expresses an objective sense of appropriateness or fairness. "妥当な金額" (a reasonable amount) is a natural and commonly used expression when assessing value, prices, or judgments, particularly in financial or evaluative contexts.

**Other Options**

② 風邪気味だったので、今日の会議が中止になったのは、私には妥当だった。  
→ I had a slight cold, so the meeting being canceled was, to me, reasonable.  
🔶 Awkward Usage  
While "妥当だった" is grammatically correct here, it sounds unnatural in a personal context. This sentence would be more naturally expressed with "当然だった" (it was expected) or "助かった" (it was a relief).

③ 旅行の日は雨の予報だったが、きれいに晴れて、妥当な天気になった。  
→ The forecast was rainy, but it cleared up nicely; the weather became reasonable.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"妥当" is not used to describe weather conditions. Weather tends to be described with terms like "いい天気" (good weather) or "運がいい" (lucky).

④ この曲は、歌詞が今の私の気持ちに妥当なので、最近よく聞いている。  
→ This song’s lyrics feel reasonable for my current feelings.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"妥当" does not express harmony or resonance with personal emotions. Better phrases would be "ぴったり合う" (fit perfectly) or "共感できる" (relatable).

**Usage Note**  
"妥当" is typically paired with words such as "金額" (amount), "判断" (judgment), or "処置" (action), and is used in situations that require logical, fair evaluations. It does not naturally apply to emotions, music, or weather, which are subjective or intuitive in nature.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 — 「품질에 비해 비싸다지만 나는 妥当(타당)하다고 생각」. 「妥当(だとう)」=타당, 적절.
오답: 2 회의 중지가 자신에게 '妥当'은 의미 불명. 3 날씨가 개어 '妥当'은 어색(「幸運·ラッキー」). 4 가사가 기분에 '妥当'은 「ぴったり」가 자연.
포인트: 「妥当な金額·妥当な判断·妥当な結論」 등 객관적 평가에.

questions.stem: かばう
opts: この団体は、海岸の清掃など、環境をかばう
この島は法律でかばわれて
弟が両親にしかられていたので、「すごく反省したよ」と言って、弟をかばった
開発した新技術をかばう
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3 is correct.

**Word Translation**  
かばう — to protect, to cover for, to defend

**Correct Sentence Translation**  
My younger brother was being scolded by our parents, so I said, "He really regrets it," to cover for him.

**Explanation**  
The word **かばう** is used to describe the act of protecting or defending someone, often in a social or personal context. In this sentence, "弟をかばった" (covered for my brother) accurately portrays the action of defending a person from blame or criticism, which is a natural usage of the word.

**Other Options**

② この島は法律で__かばわれて__いて、捕まえたり飼ったりすることは禁止されている。  
→ This island is protected by laws, and capturing or keeping things from here is prohibited.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
Using "かばう" for legal protection is unnatural. More appropriate terms would be "保護されている" (protected) or "守られている" (defended by law).

① この団体は、海岸の清掃など、環境を__かばう__活動をしている。  
→ This group engages in activities like cleaning the coast to protect the environment.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
Here, "保護する" or "守る" would be more appropriate for protecting the environment. "かばう" suits personal, direct defense rather than broader conservation efforts.

④ 開発した新技術を__かばう__ため、関連する情報を厳重に管理している。  
→ In order to protect the newly developed technology, we are strictly managing related information.  
❌ Incorrect Usage  
"かばう" is not appropriate for safeguarding technology. Instead, "保護する" or "守る" would better capture the intended meaning.

**Usage Note**  
"かばう" is most suitably used when referring to protecting people or defending someone in interpersonal contexts. It doesn't naturally extend to legal, environmental, or technological protection, where terms like "保護する" or "守る" should be used.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 — 「동생을 두둔하다(かばう)」. 「かばう」=감싸다, 두둔하다.
오답: 1 환경을 '지키다'는 「守る·保護する」. 2 법으로 보호는 「保護される」. 4 신기술을 '지키다'는 「守る·保護する」.
포인트: 「かばう」는 비판·꾸중을 받는 사람을 변호하거나, 다친 부위를 감싸는 동작에 사용.

questions.stem: 野党の追及に対し、大臣は満足な回答ができなかったどころか、質問の内容（　　　）理解できていなかった。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: すら is correct. It means "even" in English, suggesting that not even the most basic or expected action was completed.

**Question Translation**  
In response to the opposition party's questioning, not only could the minister not provide a satisfactory answer, but (he) couldn't even understand the content of the questions.

**Explanation**  
The sentence sets up a contrast or emphasis that not only was the minister unable to provide a satisfactory answer, but the situation was worse in that they couldn't "even" understand the questions. "すら" emphasizes a level of expectation, and in this context, it's used to highlight that something very basic or minimal was not achieved, thus conveying a stronger nuance.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 2: こそ**: This expresses emphasis or exclusivity, similar to "precisely" or "definitely." It would not fit the context of failing to achieve an expected understanding.
- **Answer 3: のみ**: This translates to "only" and does not convey the intended emphasis or contrast in the failure to understand even the question.
- **Answer 4: ほど**: While "ほど" is used to indicate extent or degree, it doesn't fit the grammatical structure and lacks the appropriate meaning needed to convey the element of surprise or emphasis in this context.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
すら often appears in negative contexts to indicate that something is so minimal that it is surprising or unexpected. Understanding its usage helps identify the intention of the sentence to highlight a failure to meet even the basic expectation.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 「すら」 — ~조차(도). 「Nすら〜ない」=N조차 ~않다(극단적 예).
오답: 2 こそ(~이야말로), 3 のみ(~만), 4 ほど(~만큼)는 '의외성·극단의 예' 의미가 없음.
포인트: 「どころか〜すら〜ない」 패턴 = '~하기는커녕 ~조차 ~않다'. 본문도 「回答ができなかったどころか、質問の内容すら」.

questions.stem: 最近（　　　）パソコンの調子がおかしい。この状態が続くようだったら一度修理に出したほうがよさそうだ。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: どうも is correct. It means "somehow" or "it seems that" in this context.

**Question Translation**  
Recently, the condition of my computer has been acting strange. If this state continues, it might be best to send it for repairs.

**Explanation**  
The word "どうも" is often used when the speaker is expressing an uncertain feeling or suspicion, particularly when something doesn't seem right but they can't pinpoint the exact problem. In the given sentence, "どうも" is appropriately used to convey that the computer's condition seems strange or off.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: "ちっとも" means "not at all" and is used with negative forms. It would not fit the positive description of experiencing an issue.
- Answer 2: "いったい" means "what on earth" or "indeed," typically used to emphasize a question or doubt, not to indicate a suspicion about an ongoing state.
- Answer 4: "まさか" means "no way" or "can't be," commonly used to express disbelief or surprise, which doesn't match the context of a recurring issue.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
"どうも" can imply uncertainty or suspicion when something seems amiss without clear evidence or understanding. It's frequently used to express such feelings about ongoing or observed situations that lack specific clarity.
questions.expl_ko:

오답: 1 ちっとも(전혀, 부정과 함께), 2 いったい(도대체, 의문문), 4 まさか(설마)는 본 문맥과 안 어울림.
포인트: 「どうも調子がおかしい」=어쩐지 상태가 이상하다. 막연한 인상·의심에 사용.

questions.stem:
（広告で）
川西ピアノ教室では、初心者、経験者（　　　）、どなたにでも丁寧に指導します。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: を問わず is correct. It means "regardless of" or "irrespective of."

**Question Translation**  
In the Kawanishi Piano School advertisement: "At Kawanishi Piano School, we provide careful instruction to everyone, regardless of whether you are a beginner or experienced."

**Explanation**  
The answer "を問わず" is the best fit because it is typically used to indicate that something does not matter or is not a concern for the situation, context, or decision at hand. In this sentence, the school provides instruction to anyone, no matter if they are beginners or have some experience playing the piano. The phrase emphasizes inclusivity.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: "を通して" means "through" or "via," and it's used to indicate the means or method by which something is done. It doesn't fit because the sentence isn't about using beginners or experienced players as means or channels.  
- Answer 3: "にかけて" means "over (a segment of time)" or "up to," and it's used for indicating a span or range, often of time or space. It doesn't apply here because the sentence concerns qualifications rather than time or space.  
- Answer 4: "にもかかわらず" means "despite" or "although" and is used to show contrast or opposition. It is inappropriate here as the sentence isn't contrasting two opposing situations.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
"を問わず" is a grammatical pattern used to express indifference or neutrality concerning certain conditions or attributes. It is often seen in contexts aiming to demonstrate flexibility, inclusivity, or broad applicability.

questions.stem: めったに出かけないのに、外出するとき（　　　）大雨になる。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: にかぎって is correct. It means "especially" or "particularly," and is used to emphasize that something unusual or unexpected happens only in a specific case or at a specific time.

**Question Translation**  
"I rarely go out, but on the particular occasion that I do, it always rains heavily."

**Explanation**  
"にかぎって" is used to express an exception where something unusual occurs only under specific circumstances. In this sentence, the speaker emphasizes that the rare occasion when they go out, it just so happens to rain heavily, which is an unexpected or unusual pattern.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: にあたって means "on the occasion of" or "in preparation for" and is typically used in more formal contexts dealing with preparations for events or significant changes. It does not fit the context of an occasional event with an unexpected turn.
- Answer 3: において means "in," "at," or "on," typically used to specify a location or time where something happens. It's not appropriate here as it doesn't convey the idea of something unusual happening only in specific cases.
- Answer 4: に際して means "on the occasion of" or "at the time," often used to describe something that happens right before or during a significant event. However, it does not convey the specific unexpected or ironic nuance needed in this context.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
"にかぎって" is used for emphasizing exceptions or unexpected outcomes in specific situations, often with a nuance of irony or complaint about the situation. This pattern is crucial for expressing when something occurs against expectation only under particular conditions.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 「に限(かぎ)って」 — 하필이면 ~할 때만. 「外出するときに限って大雨」=하필 외출할 때만 큰비.
오답: 1 にあたって(~을 맞아), 3 において(~에서), 4 に際して(~을 즈음하여)는 '하필이면'의 의외성 없음.
포인트: 「Nに限って」는 '하필 N에만 (운 나쁜·예외적) 일이 일어난다'는 뉘앙스.

questions.stem: 昨夜よく眠れなかった（　　　）、体がだるい。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4: せいか is correct. It means "perhaps due to" or "maybe because of."

**Question Translation**  
I feel sluggish, perhaps because I didn't sleep well last night.

**Explanation**  
The sentence is expressing a reason or cause for feeling sluggish, and "せいか" suggests that the speaker suspects the lack of sleep might be the reason. This choice conveys uncertainty and shows a subjective impression, fitting the context of guessing or surmising a reason.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1: からには** — This is often used to indicate a sense of determination or commitment, meaning "now that" or "since." It would not fit here, as the sentence doesn’t express commitment stemming from not sleeping well.
- **Answer 2: わけか** — This phrase is not used on its own in Japanese. "わけ" would imply "reason," but it needs an auxiliary verb like だ (わけだ) to form a valid expression, so this option is grammatically incorrect.
- **Answer 3: あまりに** — This means "too much" or "excessively," which doesn't appropriately link the two parts of the sentence. It's used to describe something excessive, not to indicate a cause for something else.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The phrase "せいか" is used to express a conjecture about the cause of a situation. It often implies that the speaker is unsure but sees a possible connection between the two clauses. It is commonly used in informal speech to note subjective reasoning or speculation.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 「せいか」 — ~탓인지, ~때문인지. 「眠れなかったせいか、だるい」=잠을 잘 못 잔 탓인지 나른.
오답: 1 からには(이상은), 2 わけか(있을 리), 3 あまりに(너무나)는 '추측의 원인'을 나타내지 못함.
포인트: 「せい」(부정적 원인)+「か」(불확실)=막연히 추정하는 원인.

questions.stem: 初めてこの町を訪れたが、不思議な（　　　）、ずっと前からここに住んでいるような気がする。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: ことに is correct. It means "the thing is" or "what is remarkable is."

**Question Translation**  
"I visited this town for the first time, but strangely, I have the feeling that I've been living here for a long time."

**Explanation**  
"ことに" is used to express a sense of wonder or remarkability about something, often translated as "strangely" or "remarkably." It fits the context of the sentence, where the speaker is expressing a notable feeling of familiarity despite it being their first visit.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 2: うえに** means "in addition to" or "on top of," which would suggest adding more information rather than expressing a sense of wonder. It does not fit the context of expressing a feeling.
- **Answer 3: くせに** is used to express contradiction or criticism, similar to "even though" or "despite." This implies a negative or unexpected outcome, which does not align with the sentence's intention of describing a strange feeling.
- **Answer 4: ものに** does not exist as a standalone grammatical structure that conveys the intended meaning in this context. It's an incorrect option, as it doesn't formulate a valid or relevant expression here.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The pattern "ことに" is a key grammatical structure used for expressing something noticeable or remarkable about a situation, establishing an emotional or subjective tone in the sentence. Understanding how to use these expressions can significantly impact the nuance and clarity of the statement being made.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 「ことに」 — ~하게도(감정·평가의 강조). 「不思議なことに〜」=신기하게도 ~.
오답: 2 うえに(게다가), 3 くせに(주제에), 4 ものに는 이 자리에 들어가지 않음.

questions.stem: （会社で）A「じゃ、来週の打ち合わせも水曜日でいいですか。」B「 あ、スケジュールを（　　　）ちょっとわからないので、後で連絡します。」
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: 確認してみないと is correct. It means "unless I check."

**Question Translation**  
A: "So, is next week's meeting okay on Wednesday?"  
B: "Ah, I won't know until I check the schedule, so I'll contact you later."

**Explanation**  
The phrase 確認してみないと is used to express that something must be checked to know the result. In this context, person B is saying they can't confirm the meeting date until they verify their schedule, which aligns with the expression 確認してみないと, meaning "unless I check."

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: 確認していないと suggests a negative conditional like "if I don't check," which doesn’t appropriately convey the need to check the schedule as a step to gain certainty.
- Answer 3: 確認しているか translates to "whether I am checking," which does not fit the context because it suggests ongoing or habitual action rather than the need to perform an action to confirm the schedule.
- Answer 4: 確認してみるか implies a question or a suggestion, "Shall I try to check?" This does not fit the scenario properly as it presents an unclear intention rather than the necessity of checking.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The phrase ～してみないと is commonly used in Japanese to indicate that one must attempt or do something to know the result or understand a situation, typically followed by some action resulting from that understanding or information. This is a conditional expression that provides the reason one cannot currently make a decision.
questions.expl_ko:

questions.stem: 「一つの仕事を少なくとも三年は（　　　）、どこに行っても何もできない」と言われた。
opts: やり続けられなかったら
やり続けられなくなっても
やり始められなかった
やり始められなくなっても
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: やり続けられなかったら is correct. It means "if you cannot continue doing (a job)."

**Question Translation**  
"It is said that, 'If you cannot continue doing a job for at least three years, you will not be able to do anything no matter where you go.'"

**Explanation**  
This sentence talks about the importance of persistence in a job for at least three years. The phrase "やり続けられなかったら" (if you cannot continue doing) fits perfectly because it refers to the inability to maintain or continue performing a job. The hypothetical "if" condition using "〜なかったら" (if...not) serves to express a condition under which the future action (not being able to do anything anywhere) would happen.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: やり続けられなくなっても means "even if you become unable to continue doing (a job)." The nuance here suggests that something has changed from being able to continue to not being able to, which doesn't align with the conditional requirement of persistence mentioned in the context.
  
- Answer 3: やり始められなかった means "could not start doing (a job)." This is incorrect because the context discusses continuation, not the initiation of an action.

- Answer 4: やり始められなくなっても means "even if you become unable to start doing (a job)." Like answer 3, this deals with the starting point of activity, which is irrelevant to the statement’s focus on persistence.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The key grammar pattern here is the conditional form "〜なら(ば)/たら," which implies a condition and consequence structure. Understanding the difference between actions not starting (やり始められない) and actions not continuing (やり続けられない) is crucial to selecting the correct option.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 「やり続(つづ)けられなかったら」 — 계속 해내지 못하면. 「三年は続けないと、どこに行っても何もできない」 논리.

questions.stem: 仕事でも勉強でも、一度やると決めたら最後まで（　　　）ことが大事だと思う。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: やり抜く is correct. It means "to carry through" or "to complete" something thoroughly.

**Question Translation**  
"In both work and study, I think it's important to see things through to the end once you've decided to do them."

**Explanation**  
The expression "やり抜く" (yarinuku) is used when describing the action of completing something thoroughly despite difficulties. In this sentence, it emphasizes the importance of persevering to the end once a decision is made. The context indicates determination and completion, which is why "やり抜く" fits best.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: やり直す (yarinaosu) means "to redo" or "to do again." This does not fit because the sentence is about completing tasks, not redoing them.
- Answer 2: やりだす (yaridasu) means "to start doing." This suggests the beginning of an action rather than completion, which conflicts with the context of finishing a task.
- Answer 4: やりかける (yarikakeru) means "to start and leave unfinished" or "to be half-done." This does not align with the idea of finishing something to the end, as suggested by the sentence.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The verb "やり抜く" combines "やる" (to do) with "抜く" (to pull through, to finish), creating a nuance of overcoming challenges to complete a task. This is crucial in understanding the commitment and perseverance implied by the complete sentence.
questions.expl_ko:

오답: 1 やり直す(다시 하다), 2 やりだす(시작하다), 4 やりかける(시작만 하다)는 '끝까지'와 안 맞음.
포인트: 복합동사 「V抜く」=끝까지 V하다(=「考え抜く·走り抜く」).

questions.stem: （受付で）山川「すみません。ABC社の山川と申しますが、営業部の中西さんをお願いします。」 受付「申し訳ございません。中西はただいま外出しておりますが。」山川「え、中西さんご本人から、この時間だったらいらっしゃると（　　　）が。」
opts: お聞きになったんです
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4: 伺ったんです is correct. It means "I heard" or "I was told."

**Question Translation**  
(Yamakawa at the reception)  
Yamakawa: "Excuse me. My name is Yamakawa from ABC Company. Could I please speak to Mr. Nakanishi from the Sales Department?"  
Receptionist: “I’m terribly sorry. Mr. Nakanishi is currently out.”  
Yamakawa: “Oh, I was told by Mr. Nakanishi himself that he would be here around this time.”

**Explanation**  
"伺ったんです" is the most appropriate choice as it uses the humble verb "伺う," which means "to hear" or "to ask," acknowledging that the speaker received information from a superior or someone in a respectful position. In the context of a business conversation where politeness is paramount, using a humble form like "伺った" when talking about information received from Mr. Nakanishi is suitable.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: お聞きになったんです — "お聞きになる" is a respectful form intended to refer to the listener's actions. Here, Yamakawa is the one receiving the information, not the listener, making this inappropriate.
- Answer 2: 申し上げたんです — "申し上げる" means "to say" in a humble form. It indicates that the speaker is conveying information, rather than having received it, which is contrary to Yamakawa’s actual context.
- Answer 3: ご存じなんです — "ご存じ" means "to know" in a respectful form, and it would indicate Yamakawa is aware of something rather than having been informed by Mr. Nakanishi. This does not fit the context that Yamakawa has heard from Nakanishi.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- "伺う" is a polite and humble verb used in respectful or formal situations to mean "to hear" or "to ask." It is often used when you humbly talk about your own actions in relation to someone else. This humility contrasts with "聞く," which is why it's favored here.

오답: 1 お聞きになった는 존경어(상대의 행위)라 자신의 행위에 부적절. 2 申し上げた는 '말했다'의 겸양. 3 ご存じだ는 '아시다'의 존경어.
포인트: 자신이 「中西さんから聞いた」 → 겸양 「伺った」. 비즈니스 회화 정형.

questions.stem: 就職が決まった会社に「早く働きたい」と話したら、その後連絡が来て、就職するまでの間、アルバイトを（　　　）。
opts: してあげることになった
してもらうことにした
させてあげることにした
させてもらうことになった
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 4: させてもらうことになった is correct. It means "I was allowed to work part-time" and implies a sense of receiving permission or an opportunity from someone else to do something.

**Question Translation**  
When I told the company where I had been promised a job, "I want to start working soon," they contacted me later, and I was allowed to work part-time until I officially started.

**Explanation**  
The phrase させてもらうことになった indicates that the speaker received permission from the company to work part-time. The verb form させてもらう expresses that the speaker was given the opportunity to do something by someone else, and ことになった indicates a decision made as a result of circumstances or a situation that unfolded.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: してあげることになった - This means "I ended up doing (it) for someone," which is incorrect because the context suggests the speaker is on the receiving end of an opportunity, not giving.
- Answer 2: してもらうことにした - This means "I decided to have someone do (it) for me." The speaker does not have the authority to decide; rather, they received permission.
- Answer 3: させてあげることにした - This means "I decided to let someone do (it)," which implies the speaker is allowing someone else to do something, contrary to the intended meaning where the speaker is the one being allowed to work.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The structure させてもらう is formed from させる (causative form of する, which means "to make/let someone do") combined with もらう, which means "to receive" and often indicates receiving favor or permission. This combination conveys that the speaker is being allowed to perform the action, typically by someone in a position of authority.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 「させてもらうことになった」 — (회사 측에서) 일하게 해 줘서 그렇게 됐다.
오답: 1 してあげる는 내가 호의를 베푸는 입장이라 부적절. 2 してもらう는 '~해 받다'이지만 「ことにした」(내가 결정)는 부자연. 3 させてあげる는 내가 허락하는 쪽이라 어색.
포인트: 「Vさせてもらう」=상대의 허락을 받아 V하다. 「ことになった」=(외부 결정으로) 그렇게 됨.

questions.stem: A「先輩に食事に誘われちゃって。どうしよう。行きたくないなあ」B「どうして悩むの？嫌なら（　　　）？」A「そうなんだけど、先輩だし、断りにくくない？」
opts: 断ればいいだけでしょう
断りたいだけでしょう
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 断ればいいだけでしょう is correct. It means "You just need to refuse, right?"

**Question Translation**  
A: "I've been invited to a meal by my senior. What should I do? I don’t want to go."  
B: "Why are you worried? If you don’t want to, you just need to refuse, right?"  
A: "I know, but since they're my senior, it's hard to refuse, isn’t it?"

**Explanation**  
The sentence 「断ればいいだけでしょう」 uses a grammatical structure that suggests a simple and straightforward solution to the problem—refusing the invitation. The phrase combines "〜ばいい" (should/just have to) which implies a suggested course of action, with "だけでしょう", which adds a nuance of "right?" or "isn't that the case?" It is a common phrase used for offering simple advice.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1: 断ればいいだけなの**  
  This option lacks the nuance of seeking confirmation or agreement ("でしょう" vs. "なの"). Although it's a close option, "なの" is not as fitting in asking B's opinion and lacks the politeness and engagement "でしょう" adds.

- **Answer 2: 断りたいだけなの**  
  This suggests that A merely wants to refuse but doesn't address advising or solving any problem. It also misrepresents B's role, as they're suggesting a solution, not commenting on A's feelings.

- **Answer 4: 断りたいだけでしょう**  
  Similarly, this suggests it's simply A's desire to refuse, but B is not merely commenting on A's desires—they're trying to offer advice. This phrase doesn’t align with suggesting a resolution to A's dilemma.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The pattern "〜ばいい" is a common one in Japanese that is used to suggest that if the preceding action is taken, it will lead to a solution or desired result. When combined with "だけでしょう", it turns into a friendly suggestion that seeks some sort of agreement or understanding from the listener.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 「断ればいいだけでしょう」 — 거절하면 그만이잖아. 친구에 대한 가벼운 조언.
오답: 1 「〜なの」는 여성·아동조의 단정으로 B의 권유 톤과 어색. 2·4 「断りたい」는 '거절하고 싶다'로 의미가 어긋남.
포인트: 「Vばいいだけだ」=V하기만 하면 된다. 「でしょう?」로 동의 구함.

questions.stem: もうすぐ高校卒業だ。この学校で先生や友達と過ごす______ ______ ★ ______。
questions.expl:
**Answer (★ Position)**  
Answer 3: のも

**Correct Order**  
3 → 1 → 2 → 4  
📌 のも → あと数週間 → と思うと → 寂しさが増してくる

**Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown**  
③ のも — nominaliser; turns a preceding action or state into the subject/topic of reflection  
① あと数週間 — “only a few more weeks”; indicates the remaining time frame  
② と思うと — “when I think (that) …”; introduces a reflection leading to an emotional response  
④ 寂しさが増してくる — “sadness starts to grow”; describes the emotional response to the thought

**Reconstructed Sentence**  
もうすぐ高校卒業だ。この学校で先生や友達と過ごす**のも、あと数週間と思うと、寂しさが増してくる。**  
→ “I’ll be graduating from high school soon. When I think that I have only a few more weeks left to spend here with my teachers and friends, the sadness starts to grow.”

**Why This Order Works**  
1. **のも** nominalises the act of spending time with teachers and friends, allowing it to be considered a subject of reflection.  
2. **あと数週間** defines the limited time left, which is crucial for the reflective mood.  
3. **と思うと** connects this reflection to the subsequent emotional impact.  
4. **寂しさが増してくる** naturally follows as the consequence of thinking about the limited time.

**Why Other Orders Fail**  
- Starting with あと数週間 without a nominalised clause leaves no subject for the emotional transition, disrupting the sentence flow.  
- Placing 寂しさが増してくる too early dismisses the necessary buildup and context in the reflection.  
- と思うと requires a complete thought (nominalised clause) beforehand, so it cannot start the sentence.

**How to Solve (Quick Tip)**  
Look for:  
1. A nominalising element (like のも) to introduce a topic of reflection.  
2. Temporal or conditional phrases like あと数週間 that set the scene for the reflection.  
3. Logical connectors (like と思うと) that link the reflection to an emotional or logical result.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 (★자리=두 번째 「あと数週間」). 순서: のも→あと数週間→と思うと→寂しさが増してくる.
포인트: 「過ごすのも+あと数週間+と思うと」 = 보낼 시간도 앞으로 몇 주뿐이라 생각하니. 「Nと思うと」(~라 생각하니)의 정형.

questions.stem: Ａ「サラリーマンから農家______ ______ ★ ______があるんだね。」　Ｂ「自分の夢をどうしてもあきらめきれなくてね。」
questions.expl:
Answer (★ Position)
Answer 3: ずいぶん

Correct Order
4 → 2 → 3 → 1
📌 になる → とは → ずいぶん → 勇気

Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown
④ になる — “(to) become”; completes サラリーマンから農家[になる].
② とは — quotative-topic marker; frames the preceding clause for evaluation/exclamation.
③ ずいぶん — “quite; considerably”; adverb modifying 勇気.
① 勇気 — “courage”; pairs with がある to form “have courage.”

Reconstructed Sentence
Ａ: 「サラリーマンから**農家になるとは、ずいぶん勇気**があるんだね。」
→ “To go from a company employee to a farmer — that sure takes a lot of courage, huh.”

Why This Order Works
**〜になる＋とは** sets up an evaluative/exclamatory comment about the fact stated. **ずいぶん** naturally modifies **勇気**, and **勇気がある** states the judgment.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 (★자리=세 번째 「ずいぶん」). 순서: になる→とは→ずいぶん→勇気. 완성: 「サラリーマンから農家になるとは、ずいぶん勇気があるんだね」.
포인트: 「〜とは」(~라니)는 놀람·평가의 화제 제시. 「ずいぶん+명사」 부사 수식.

questions.stem: 遠足の日の朝、娘は、「いってきます」と ______ ______ ★ ______ 飛び出していった。
questions.expl:
Answer (★ Position)
Answer 4: のうちに

Correct Order
2 → 1 → 4 → 3
📌 言い終わるか → 終わらないか → のうちに → 玄関を

Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown
② 言い終わるか — “whether she finishes saying”; first half of the fixed pattern V-るかV-ないかのうちに
① 終わらないか — “or not finish”; second half of the pair
④ のうちに — “the instant / as soon as”; completes the pattern meaning “scarcely had (she) finished when …”
③ 玄関を — object for 飛び出していった (“dash out the front door”)

Reconstructed Sentence
遠足の日の朝、娘は、「いってきます」と**言い終わるか終わらないかのうちに、玄関を**飛び出していった。
→ “On the morning of the field trip, my daughter dashed out the door almost before she even finished saying ‘I’m off!’”

Why This Order Works
The fixed grammar **V-るかV-ないかのうちに** expresses ‘as soon as/scarcely … when’. Here, 言い終わる pairs with 終わらない, then のうちに completes the pattern; 玄関を directly precedes 飛び出していった to form “dash out the entrance.”
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 (★자리=네 번째 「のうちに」). 순서: 言い終わるか→終わらないか→のうちに→玄関を.
포인트: 「V-るかV-ないかのうちに」=V하자마자(말이 끝나기가 무섭게). 「玄関を飛び出していった」로 이어짐.

questions.stem: 参考書を読んで完璧に ______ ______ ★ ______ ということがよくある。
questions.expl:
Answer (★ Position)
Answer 2: 問題を解いてみると

Correct Order
1 → 4 → 2 → 3
📌 理解した → つもりでも → 問題を解いてみると → できない

Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown
① 理解した — “(I) understood”; base for the concessive pattern
④ つもりでも — “even if I *think* I did / intend/assume I did”; concessive
② 問題を解いてみると — “when I try solving problems”; sets the condition for realization
③ できない — “(I) can’t do (them)”; the result

Reconstructed Sentence
参考書を読んで完璧に**理解したつもりでも、問題を解いてみると、できない**ということがよくある。
→ “Even when I feel I’ve understood perfectly from the reference book, I often find I can’t do it when I try the problems.”

Why This Order Works
**Vたつもりでも** marks a mistaken assumption, followed by **〜てみると** to show the reality found upon trying; **できない** states the unexpected outcome.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 (★자리=두 번째 「問題を解いてみると」). 순서: 理解した→つもりでも→問題を解いてみると→できない.
포인트: 「Vたつもりでも」=V한 셈치고 있어도(자기 인식과 현실의 어긋남). 결론은 「できない」.

questions.expl:
Answer (★ Position)
Answer 4: １００年以上生きる

Correct Order
2 → 3 → 4 → 1
📌 すむ → 魚の中には → １００年以上生きる → ものもいる

Chunk-by-Chunk Breakdown
② すむ — modifies 魚 (“fish that live [here]”)
③ 魚の中には — “among the fish …”; topicalises a subset
④ １００年以上生きる — “that live for over 100 years”; relative clause modifying もの
① ものもいる — “there are some (such ones)”; completes the predicate

Reconstructed Sentence
この池に**すむ魚の中には、１００年以上生きるものもいる**そうだ。
→ “It’s said that among the fish living in this pond, some live for over 100 years.”

Why This Order Works
Modifier order is **[V-plain] + 魚 → 中には → [relative clause] + もの → いる**. 「すむ」 first narrows the set to fish living in this pond; 「１００年以上生きる」 modifies もの, and 「もいる」 states existence of such examples.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 (★자리=세 번째 「１００年以上生きる」). 순서: すむ→魚の中には→１００年以上生きる→ものもいる.
포인트: 「Nの中には〜ものもいる」(N 가운데에는 ~한 것도 있다) 정형. 「すむ」가 「魚」를 수식.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: 気になるもの is correct. It means "something that is of concern."

**Question Translation**  
In everyday life, weather forecasts are indispensable information. When choosing clothes to wear or planning activities for the weekend, weather is [48]. Many people probably check the weather forecast every morning.

**Explanation**  
The sentence context suggests that weather is something people consistently pay attention to or are concerned about when making decisions in their daily lives. The phrase 気になるもの (something that is of concern or of interest) aligns perfectly with this context. It implies the importance and relevance of weather information in decision-making processes such as choosing outfits or planning events.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: 気になるだけ means "only concerned." Using "only" here implies a limitation that changes the meaning to something less relevant about the weather’s impact, which doesn’t match the intended emphasis on the importance of weather.
- Answer 3: 気になるかどうか translates to "whether it is of concern or not." This choice introduces an unnecessary element of uncertainty that doesn’t fit the explanatory tone of the sentence, which leans towards certainty in weather's importance.
- Answer 4: 気になるかのよう translates to "as if it is of concern." This implies a hypothetical scenario, suggesting weather may not actually be important, distorting the original message.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
気になる (きになる) is a common expression used to express interest or concern. もの (もの) translates to "thing" or "matter," often used to make generalizations or broad references. Recognizing how these structures work together to emphasize the notion of concern or interest is key for this question type.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 「気になるもの」 — 신경 쓰이는 것. 「天気は〜だ」의 명사 술어.
오답: 2 だけ는 '~만'으로 의미가 약함. 3 かどうか는 의문이라 단정문에 어색. 4 かのよう는 비유로 단정과 안 맞음.
포인트: 「Nは(かなり)気になるものだ」=N은 (꽤) 신경 쓰이는 법이다. 일반화 표현.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: そこで is correct. It means "therefore" or "so" to indicate a logical conclusion or action based on the previous information.

**Question Translation**  
The government has started an initiative to make advanced demand forecasts using meteorological data and POS data (which indicates what was sold, when, how many, and at what price), providing it to manufacturers and retailers. As a result, not only can food loss be reduced, but carbon dioxide emissions generated during the disposal process can also be decreased.

**Explanation**  
"そこで" is used to suggest a logical continuation or outcome from the previous sentence. Here, it closely ties the initiative of using weather data and sales data to the potential outcomes. The text discusses a method to reduce food loss through better demand forecasting. Thus, "そこで" fits well to indicate this logical progression in the initiatives taken by the government.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: "なお" means "furthermore" or "in addition," which is unsuitable for indicating a logical result derived from previously mentioned actions; it typically adds extra information, not a direct outcome.
- Answer 2: "たとえば" means "for example," which is used to illustrate a point with an example, not to indicate a consequence or logical step based on prior statements.
- Answer 4: "ところが" means "however" or "on the contrary," used for contrasting statements or unexpected results. It doesn’t match the context of drawing a conclusion from an initiative.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
"そこで" is a conjunctive adverb used effectively to show cause and effect or to present the next step resulting logically from earlier information. It's important for connecting ideas smoothly in more formal and written Japanese contexts.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 「そこで」 — 그래서. 앞 문장(수요 예측 실수→식품 손실)을 받아 '그래서 정부가 착수'.
오답: 1 なお(덧붙여), 2 たとえば(예컨대), 4 ところが(그런데, 역접)는 인과 흐름과 안 맞음.
포인트: 「そこで」=문제 제시→대응 행동의 접속사. 본문 구조 정확히 표시.

questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: この取り組みは is correct. It means "this initiative" or "this effort."

**Question Translation**  
Therefore, an experiment was conducted focusing on "tofu," which cannot be stored for long and whose sales are greatly affected by weather conditions, and "noodle soup" (mentsuyu), which has demand concentrated in specific seasons. 

**Explanation**  
The keyword "この取り組みは" means "this initiative" or "this effort," referring to the initiative discussed in the preceding text. The entire passage explains a new initiative utilizing weather forecasts to improve food demand predictions and reduce food waste. Using "この" (this) specific reference points to the discussion at hand, covering that the experiment discussed is part of the initiative.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: そういった取り組み means "such efforts" and is generally used to refer to a concept introduced but not immediately preceding in detail. "そういった" implies a generalizing distance not fitting here.
- Answer 3: あのような取り組み means "such an initiative as that," generally used away from the context of the current discussion.
- Answer 4: どちらの取り組みも means "either initiative," which is incorrect because only one specific effort has been mentioned for detailed discussion.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The usage of demonstratives such as "この" (this) is crucial in the preceding sentence's context. Correctly identifying these key phrases can drastically change comprehension, specifically where simplification of comparative terms is used.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 「この取り組みは」 — 이 활동은. 앞에 나온 정부의 새 활동을 가리킨다.
오답: 2 そういった는 막연한 범주화로 단일 활동 지칭에 약함. 3 あのような는 화자·청자 모두 멀리 있는 것. 4 どちらの〜も는 양자택일 대상이 없음.
포인트: 직전 단락의 구체적 단일 대상→「この」가 가장 자연.

opts: 期待できるはずだった
期待できればよかった
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: 期待できるそうだ is correct. It means "it is expected" or "it seems it can be expected."

**Question Translation**  
In the future, greater achievements are expected.

**Explanation**  
The passage discusses the positive results of using weather data for food demand forecasts and the potential to reduce food waste. Phrases like "減らせることがわかった" (it was found that it can be reduced) demonstrate ongoing positive outcomes and expectations for further reductions. The choice "期待できるそうだ" conveys a neutral, third-party perspective on future expectations, which aligns with the informative style of the newspaper column. This fits naturally with the discussion about anticipated improvements and future potential based on current progress.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: 期待できるからだ means "because it is expected," focusing on causality, unsuitable without a preceding context stating something happened because of these expectations.
- Answer 3: 期待できるはずだった translates as "was supposed to be expected," implying an expectation that was not met, which contradicts the ongoing positive theme of future achievements in the text.
- Answer 4: 期待できればよかった means "it would have been good if it could be expected," suggesting regret or missed potential, which doesn’t fit the positive forecast of the passage.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The phrase "期待できるそうだ" uses the particle "そうだ," which is commonly used to indicate hearsay or something that is expected based on what has been reported, fitting the tone of a newspaper article reporting on future developments. Recognizing contexts in which "そうだ" indicates projections or expectations is useful for understanding its application in texts.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 「期待できるそうだ」 — 기대할 수 있다고 한다(전문). 칼럼·기사의 인용 마무리.
오답: 1 からだ는 이유 설명으로 문맥과 안 맞음. 3 はずだった는 '예정이었다(빗나감)'. 4 ばよかった는 반사실 후회.
포인트: 신문 칼럼의 일반적 결말 패턴 「〜そうだ(전문)」.

questions.stem: 筆者の考えに合うのはどれか。
opts: 大人は子供の好き嫌いを気にしすぎない方が良い。
大人の食べ物に対する態度が、子供の好き嫌いに影響する。
子供の頃の好き嫌いは、大人になってからも変わらない。
子供の好き嫌いを無くすより、食事を楽しむことの方が大切だ。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: 大人の食べ物に対する態度が、子供の好き嫌いに影響する。 It means "The attitude of adults towards food influences the likes and dislikes of children."

**Question Translation**  
Which option matches the author's opinion?

**Explanation**  
In the passage, the author discusses how children's preferences are influenced by the attitudes of adults, especially parents. If adults consistently express dislike for certain foods, children are likely to share that sentiment. On the other hand, when adults positively engage with food, even if children initially struggle with it, the positive display can spark interest and eventually lead children to enjoy those foods. This idea directly aligns with Answer 2, which focuses on the influence of adult attitudes on children's food preferences.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1:** 大人は子供の好き嫌いを気にしすぎない方が良い (Adults should not worry too much about children's likes and dislikes.)  
  This option is incorrect because the passage doesn't suggest ignoring children's preferences but rather influencing them through positive demonstration.
  
- **Answer 3:** 子供の頃の好き嫌いは、大人になってからも変わらない (Likes and dislikes from childhood do not change into adulthood.)  
  The passage doesn't support this idea. Instead, it emphasizes that children's preferences can change based on adult influence.
  
- **Answer 4:** 子供の好き嫌いを無くすより、食事を楽しむことの方が大切だ (Enjoying meals is more important than eliminating food dislikes.)  
  While the passage mentions using fun and enjoyment as a method to address picky eating, it does not suggest that enjoyment is more important than addressing food preferences.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- **偏食 (へんしょく):** Meaning "picky eating" or "unbalanced diet," indicating the selective or limited range of food one chooses to eat.
- **興味が湧く (きょうみがわく):** "To become interested" or "to develop interest," relevant in describing how children's interest in foods can develop positively when adults model positive behavior.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 — 어른의 음식에 대한 태도가 아이의 호불호에 영향을 준다.
근거: 「保護者が嫌いなものは、子供も好きになれない」, 「周囲の大人たちが『美味しいね』と笑顔で食べている姿を見て興味が湧く」.
오답: 1은 「気にしすぎない」이 본문에 없음. 3 평생 변하지 않는다는 언급 없음. 4 즐기는 것이 더 중요하다는 비교는 본문 취지가 아님.

questions.stem: このメールで伝えたいことは何か。
opts: 誰でも駐車場利用できるようにしてほしい。
自転車を止めるスペースを広げてほしい。
駐車場をしっかり管理してほしい。
管理人の人数を増やしてほしい。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 駐車場をしっかり管理してほしい is correct. It means "I want the parking lot to be properly managed."

**Question Translation**  
What does this email intend to convey?

**Explanation**  
The passage describes a complaint regarding bicycles parked without a proper permit at a paid parking lot, creating inconvenience for those who have paid. The writer requests that the parking lot management ensure that only those who pay can park there by taking specific actions like warning unauthorized users and clearing improperly parked bicycles. This indicates a desire for the parking lot to be managed more effectively, matching answer 3's focus on proper management.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: 誰でも駐車場利用できるようにしてほしい means "I want anyone to be able to use the parking lot." The email complains about unauthorized parking, so allowing more open access contradicts the request for stricter management.
- Answer 2: 自転車を止めるスペースを広げてほしい means "I want the space for parking bicycles to be expanded." The complaint isn't about the amount of space, but rather about improper usage, so expanding space doesn't address the issue.
- Answer 4: 管理人の人数を増やしてほしい means "I want the number of managers to be increased." While the email mentions a manager should inspect the area, it doesn't specifically request more staff, but rather effective management practices.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The term 無断で止められている (unpermitted parking) and the action 片付ける (to clear) focus on unauthorized use and the need for rectification, highlighting the theme of management needing improvement. Understanding these nuances helps in identifying the intent behind the writer's request for proper coordination.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 — 주차장을 제대로 관리해 달라.
근거: 「管理人が見回って、これらの自転車を片付けたり、無断で止めている人に注意したりするべき」, 「適切な対応をお願いします」.
오답: 1 누구나 이용은 본문과 반대(허가제). 2 공간 확장은 언급 없음. 4 관리인 증원은 구체적 요구가 아님.

questions.stem: この人がコンビニで売られている飲みものを見て気づいたことは何か。
opts: 飲み物が売れる理由には、持ち運びしやすいかどうかも関係すること。
量がすくなくなっても値段の安い物の方が売れるようになったこと。
ペットボトルの飲み物で減量する女性が昨年辺りから増えていること。
どのような飲み物が流行るかは、人気のある雑誌の影響を受けること。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: 飲み物が売れる理由には、持ち運びしやすいかどうかも関係すること. It means that the reason for the sale of drinks is related to whether they are easy to carry.

**Question Translation**  
What did this person notice about the drinks sold at the convenience store?

**Explanation**  
In the passage, the author notes that drink sizes have decreased from what is usually expected (500cc) to around 400cc, but the price has remained the same. Despite the drink being seemingly more expensive due to the reduced size, it remains popular. The reason provided for this popularity is that the smaller size is easier for women to carry in their bags. This directly matches Answer 1, which explains that the ease of carrying is a factor in why drinks are sold.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2 suggests that cheaper drinks with less quantity are selling more, which is incorrect. The passage says the price is the same despite a reduction in size.
- Answer 3 implies that women are drinking these beverages to reduce their weight (diet), but the passage actually discusses the decrease in bottle size, not weight loss.
- Answer 4 claims the popularity of drinks is influenced by popular magazines, but the passage doesn't mention magazines affecting drink trends; magazines were only mentioned as something the author looks at in the store.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- 凝縮（ぎょうしゅく）: This kanji word means "condensed" or "concentrated," indicating that various societal trends can be observed from a single product — drinks in this context.
- 割高（わりだか）: Refers to something being relatively expensive for its quantity, used to describe that although the drink became smaller, the price remained the same, making it appear expensive.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 — 음료가 팔리는 이유에는 휴대 용이성도 관계한다.
근거: 「400cc前後に減量している〜割高なようだが結構人気がある〜女性がバッグに入れやすい」 → 휴대성이 매출에 영향.
오답: 2 가격이 더 싼 게 아니라 같음(割高이라 오히려 비쌈). 3 다이어트 언급 없음. 4 잡지 영향 언급 없음.

questions.stem: このメールの用件は何か。
opts: 注文した商品の数を、１０台に変更できるかどうか教えてほしい。
注文した商品の一部を、１９日までに納品できるかどうか教えてほしい。
注文した商品のすべてを、１９日までに納品できるかどうか教えてほしい。
注文した商品のすべてを、キャンセルできるかどうか教えてほしい。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 2: 注文した商品の一部を、１９日までに納品できるかどうか教えてほしい is correct. It means "Can you let me know if a part of the ordered products can be delivered by the 19th?"

**Question Translation**  
What is the business matter of this email?

**Explanation**  
The passage states that the delivery is delayed but emphasizes the necessity of having at least 10 units delivered before the day the sale begins, which is on the 20th. Therefore, the email is specifically inquiring whether part of the order (at least 10 units) can be delivered by the 19th, aligning with the event requirements mentioned.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 1: "注文した商品の数を、１０台に変更できるかどうか教えてほしい" suggests a request to change the order quantity to 10 units, which doesn’t match the passage. The email doesn’t ask to alter the order quantity but asks for a partial delivery.
- Answer 3: "注文した商品のすべてを、１９日までに納品できるかどうか教えてほしい" asks if the entire order can be delivered by the 19th. The passage only requests at least 10 units by this date, not the full amount.
- Answer 4: "注文した商品のすべてを、キャンセルできるかどうか教えてほしい" implies an inquiry about canceling the entire order. Although the passage mentions the possibility of canceling if deadlines aren't met, the main request focuses on the possibility of delivering part of the order before the sale, making this choice inaccurate.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
The phrase "納品" (のうひん) means “delivery,” referring specifically to the receipt of ordered goods. Understanding such key words is crucial to accurately interpreting business-related inquiries often found in professional correspondence.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 2번 — 주문한 상품 일부를 19일까지 납품 가능한지 알려 주기 바람.
근거: 「セールが始まる前日(=19日)までに、少なくとも10台は納品していただけないでしょうか」(부분 납품 요청), 「至急ご回答いただきたく」.
오답: 1 「변경」이 아니라 일부 선납 요청. 3 '전부'가 아니라 '적어도 10대'. 4 취소는 최후의 가능성일 뿐 주 용건이 아님.

questions.stem: この調査結果では、就職先を決めるとき最も多くの学生が重視していた点は何か。
opts: 働いている人たちやその職場の印象がいいこと。
自分が希望している職種に就くことができること。
将来その企業が発展する可能性を持っていること。
勤務地が選択でき、転勤の可能性が少ないこと。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 1: 働いている人たちやその職場の印象がいいこと is correct. It means "The impression of the people working there and the workplace is favorable."

**Question Translation**  
In this survey result, what was the point that most students considered important when deciding on a job placement?

**Explanation**  
The passage discusses a student awareness survey about job selection criteria. The most emphasized factor for choosing a company, with 54.3% of students mentioning it, was "社員の魅力や社内の雰囲気," meaning "the charm of the employees and the atmosphere within the company." This directly corresponds to Answer 1, which refers to the impression and feeling of the workplace and its employees.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- Answer 2: 自分が希望している職種に就くことができること means "being able to get the job type one desires." Though "希望職種に就ける可能性" (possibility to get desired job type) is mentioned in the passage, it is not the top factor; it's suppressed by the main factor described in Answer 1.
- Answer 3: 将来その企業が発展する可能性を持っていること means "having the potential to develop in the future." This refers to "将来性" (future potential), which was considered but didn't top the list.
- Answer 4: 勤務地が選択でき、転勤の可能性が少ないこと means "being able to choose the location and having low transfer probability." "勤務地や転勤の有無" (location and transfer presence) was also considered by 22.1% of students, but it was not the most significant factor.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- 重視する (じゅうしする) means "to consider important" or "to prioritize."
- The survey uses compound phrases like "社員の魅力" (employee appeal) and "良好な人間関係" (favorable human relations), showing nuances in what students value when selecting a workplace. Recognizing such phrases helps understand how preference priorities are articulated in Japanese.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 1번 — 일하는 사람들이나 직장의 인상이 좋은 것.
근거: 「『社員の魅力や社内の雰囲気』(54.3%)」가 톱.
오답: 2 희망 직종은 본문에서 '뒤로 밀린' 요인. 3 장래성도 마찬가지로 추월된 요인. 4 근무지·전근(22.1%)은 2위.

questions.stem: 筆者が編集者の仕事を重要だと考えるのはなぜか。
opts: 編集者は読者の求めているものがわかるから。
編集者は具体的なアドバイスをくれるから。
編集者の反応次第で意欲が変わるから。
編集者の反応から面白い考えを思いつくから。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**  
Answer 3: 編集者の反応次第で意欲が変わるから. It means "Because the writer's motivation changes depending on the editor's reaction."

**Question Translation**  
Why does the author consider the editor's job important?

**Explanation**  
The passage highlights that the editor plays a significant role in the writing process for the author. In the process, the author writes with the editor as the initial audience and notes that the editor’s reactions can significantly impact the author's motivation. This underscores why the author considers the editor's role crucial, making answer 3 correct because it directly aligns with how the author describes the influence of an editor's reaction on their motivation.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**  
- **Answer 1**: 編集者は読者の求めているものがわかるから (Because editors understand what readers want). This option is incorrect because the passage does not discuss the editor's understanding of reader preferences as a reason for their importance.

- **Answer 2**: 編集者は具体的なアドバイスをくれるから (Because editors provide specific advice). While editors may give advice, the passage doesn’t focus on this as the main reason for their importance. The focus is more on their impact on the author's motivation through their reactions.

- **Answer 4**: 編集者の反応から面白い考えを思いつくから (Because the author comes up with interesting ideas from the editor's reactions). This choice inaccurately describes the influence because the passage doesn't mention that the editor's reactions lead to new ideas. It is rather about how those reactions affect the author's motivation.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**  
- 念頭に置く (ねんとうにおく): Literally "to place in mind," meaning "to bear in mind" or "be mindful of," is used to denote that the author writes with the editor consciously in their thoughts.
- 意欲 (いよく): This refers to motivation or will, describing the author's drive to write, which is influenced by the editor's feedback.  
Understanding the nuance and implication of such phrases is key to comprehending the author's reasoning in this passage.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 3번 — 편집자의 반응에 따라 (필자의) 의욕이 변하기 때문.
근거: 「編集者がつまらない反応をしそうだと、こちらのやる気も落ちてくる〜逆に言うと、編集者とはそれくらい重要な仕事」.
오답: 1 독자의 요구를 안다는 언급은 없음. 2 구체적 조언은 본문에 안 나옴. 4 재미있는 생각이 떠오른다는 인과는 본문이 아님.

questions.stem: 筆者によると、学生のレポートがつまらなかったのはなぜか。
opts: よいレポートを書かなければいけないと思い込んで書いたから。
教師の反応を気にして、頭が固くなってしまったから。
授業でした質問の答えを生かして書かなかったから。
具体的な相手を意識して書かなかったから。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**
Answer 4 is correct. It means "Because they didn’t write with a specific reader in mind."

**Question Translation**
"According to the author, why were the student’s reports boring?"

**Explanation**
In class, the student asked interesting questions because he was speaking to a **concrete other** (the teacher). But when writing the report, he adopted an impersonal, general style and lost that sense of addressing someone specific, so his thinking became rigid and the report became dull.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**
1. よいレポートを書かなければいけないと思い込んで書いたから。— "Because they were convinced they had to write a good report." ❌
→ The text stresses **loss of a concrete addressee**, not perfectionism itself.

2. 教師の反応を気にして、頭が固くなってしまったから。— "Because they worried about the teacher’s reaction and became stiff." ❌
→ The passage doesn’t say fear of the teacher; it contrasts speaking **to** the teacher (good) vs. writing generally (bad).

3. 授業でした質問の答えを生かして書かなかったから。— "Because they didn’t make use of answers from class questions." ❌
→ Not mentioned; the issue is audience and style, not using specific Q&A content.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**
「具体的な他者に向かって」= addressing a specific person; 「一般論みたいに書く」= to write as if stating general theory (impersonal style).
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 — 구체적인 상대를 의식하지 않고 썼기 때문.
근거: 질문할 때는 「具体的な他者、すなわち私に向かってしゃべっている」가 흥미로웠지만, 레포트는 「一般論」을 향하느라 재미를 잃었다.
오답: 1·2 압박이나 경직은 본문이 아님. 3 질문의 답을 활용 여부는 논점이 아님.

questions.stem: 筆者によると、本や論文を書くうえで大切なことは何か。
opts: 語りかけるようなスタイルで書く。
書きたいと思うことだけを書く。
読み手にとって意味のあることを書く。
読み手に向かって語りたいことを書く。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**
Answer 4 is correct. It means "Write what you genuinely want to speak **to the reader** about."

**Question Translation**
"According to the author, what is important when writing books and papers?"

**Explanation**
The author says that even if the final style seems impersonal, writing needs **dialogue**. You should write things you’d feel like telling someone. Hence, what you want to **address to a reader** is crucial.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**
1. 語りかけるようなスタイルで書く。— "Write in a conversational style." ❌
→ Style alone isn’t the point; the key is **having something to address to someone**, not necessarily casual tone.

2. 書きたいと思うことだけを書く。— "Write only what you want to write." ❌
→ Self-centered desire isn’t enough; it must be content you’d want to tell **someone** (dialogic).

3. 読み手にとって意味のあることを書く。— "Write things meaningful to the reader." ❌
→ Close, but the text emphasizes **talk-worthiness and dialogue**, not abstract ‘meaningfulness’. Option 4 captures this nuance directly.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**
「対話がないといけない」= there must be dialogue; 「人に話したくなるようなこと」= something you feel like telling people.
questions.expl_ko:
정답: 4번 — 독자를 향해 말하고 싶은 것을 쓴다.
근거: 본문의 일관된 주장 — 글쓰기는 결국 '구체적 상대(독자)에게 말하듯' 쓰는 것이 중요.
오답: 1 '말하는 듯한 스타일'은 형식의 문제일 뿐. 2 '쓰고 싶은 것만'은 독자 고려를 빠뜨림. 3 '독자에게 의미 있는 것'은 가깝지만, 본문 강조는 '말하고 싶다'는 화자 측 의식.

questions.stem: 好きなことしかやりたがらない子供をつくってしまったとあるが、筆者はどこにその原因があるかと考えているか。
opts: 個性の重視ということが間違って解釈されている点。
個性の重視ということが注目されている点。
個性の意味についての解釈が定まっていない点。
教師が社会生活上のルールを教えていない点。
questions.expl:
**Correct Answer**
Answer 1 is correct. It means "The point is that ‘respecting individuality’ has been **misinterpreted**."

**Question Translation**
"It says ‘we ended up creating children who only want to do what they like.’ Where does the author think the cause lies?"

**Explanation**
The passage explains that a **mistaken interpretation** of ‘respecting individuality’—letting children freely do only what they want—spread, which led to children who want to do only what they like and to lost chances to teach social customs.

**Why Other Options Are Incorrect**
2. 個性の重視ということが注目されている点。— "The fact that emphasis on individuality is attracting attention." ❌
→ Attention itself isn’t the problem; the **misreading** is.

3. 個性の意味についての解釈が定まっていない点。— "The interpretation of individuality isn’t settled." ❌
→ The author points to a **specific wrong interpretation**, not mere lack of consensus.

4. 教師が社会生活上のルールを教えていない点。— "Teachers aren’t teaching social rules." ❌
→ This is presented as a **consequence** of the misinterpretation, not the root cause.

**Grammar/Vocabulary Note**
「解釈が広がりました」= a certain interpretation spread; 「～してしまった」 conveys an unintended negative outcome.
